description: Earth data is mostly visual, making environmental trends harder to explore, especially for people with visual impairments. Earth in Harmony turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into an interactive musical journey. Visitors follow a guided story, then scan ocean regions and compare dates, hearing sea-surface temperature anomalies as changing melodies, harmonies, and rhythms.
summary:
Terraphony is a web-based “listening atlas” for NASA Space Apps 2026’s Earth Information Jukebox challenge. It turns real NASA Earth observations into music you can explore, understand, and save as your own Earth Record.

Two journeys bring the data to life:

Ocean in Motion: Draw a route across the sea. At 24 stops, hear daily sea-surface temperatures from NASA JPL’s MUR SST dataset, alongside NASA SVS 3912 ocean imagery.

A Year in One Place: Choose any land location. Hear 23 notes representing 16-day windows of plant greenness from NASA’s 2023 MODIS NDVI data, while dated satellite imagery changes with the music.

Higher values produce higher notes; missing or cloud-covered data become silent rests, never invented measurements. Strings, horns, harp, and timpani enrich the melody. An optional Beethoven-guided narrated tour makes exploration approachable. Select any note to reveal its value, units, location, date, and musical mapping.

Terraphony makes Earth science tangible: hear changes along the Gulf Stream or seasonal patterns in the Nile Delta, then learn what the observations can—and cannot—tell us. Export your Earth Record as an image, audio file, or reproducible recipe, grounded in the same NASA measurements.
details:
Terraphony, Earth's Unwritten Symphony
Every place has a rhythm. Every change has a story.

Team: Amira El-Garf, Chahd Ihab, Mahmoud Abbas
Challenge: The Earth Information Jukebox — NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Why Terraphony?

NASA's Earth observations reveal changes in our oceans and landscapes, but scientific datasets and visualizations can be difficult to interpret, especially without a technical background. Terraphony offers another way in: a listening atlas that turns real measurements into music without hiding the science.

Visitors choose a place, hear the observations, watch the corresponding NASA visuals, and investigate the source of any note. They can then turn their journey into a personal Earth Record. The live web application and short project demo show how the experience works for curious visitors, students, educators, and people with different sensory preferences.

Ocean in Motion

Visitors draw a path across the ocean or choose a suggested route, such as the Gulf Stream. Using d3-geo and TopoJSON, the application resamples the path into 24 geographical stops. Each stop is mapped to a sea-surface temperature from NASA JPL's MUR SST v4.1, accessed through the NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP mirror. Python, NumPy, SciPy, and Pillow help prepare and validate the ocean data and imagery alignment.

During playback, the scanner and Living Score follow the route over date-matched frames from NASA SVS 3912. The notes use observation-based MUR temperatures, while the visualization uses the ECCO2 ocean model; these are different NASA products, identified separately in the app.

The current prototype supports 18 August 2007 and 6 February 2008, using a 0.25° MUR subset rather than the entire original grid.

A Year in One Place

Visitors select any land location on the map or enter coordinates. Terraphony retrieves 23 sixteen-day windows from 2023 using NASA MODIS/Terra MOD13Q1 v061 through the NASA ORNL DAAC web service. The NDVI observations describe vegetation greenness and become a seasonal melody.

For each window, the system checks a 9 × 9 pixel neighborhood; a note is used only when at least 50% of the pixels satisfy the accepted quality criteria. Otherwise, that window becomes a rest. Dated NASA GIBS imagery changes with the music, so visitors can see as well as hear the annual pattern. NDVI indicates greenness, not plant health on its own.

From measurements to music

Terraphony maps sea-surface temperature (−2 to 31°C) and NDVI (0 to 0.9) onto a fixed 11-note range, C3–C5. Higher measurements produce higher notes. Missing or quality-rejected observations produce silence, not invented data. The original numeric value remains available even when multiple measurements share a note.

A custom engine built with the Web Audio API and Web Workers renders the composition without blocking the interactive map. Strings, horns, harp, timpani, and bass enrich the data melody; the app distinguishes measurement-driven notes from artistic accompaniment. The music is rule-based, not generative AI.

The Living Score stays accessible during exploration. Selecting a note reveals its value, units, place, date, source, and mapping rule; land observations also show pixel quality information. See the scientific methodology for reproducibility details.

Guided and accessible exploration

An optional fictional Beethoven companion introduces the two journeys and explains discoveries. The guided tour advances after one start action; visitors can pause, replay, skip, or explore on their own. In-app speech uses the browser's Speech Synthesis API, accompanied by visible captions.

The interface also provides keyboard access to the Living Score, text explanations, visual alternatives to musical events, reduced-motion support, and responsive layouts. These features offer complementary ways to engage with the same observations rather than assuming everyone learns through sound or sight alone.

Make My Earth Record

After exploring a route or a year, visitors can press their observations into a personal Earth Record. A transition turns the sampled data into a score, then a record groove and custom sleeve artwork derived from that journey.

They can export the sleeve as PNG, the composition as WAV, or a JSON recipe containing observations and settings so the record can be reconstructed and checked. This turns a scientific exploration into something visitors can revisit and share.

Engineering, scope, and next steps

The application is built with React 18, TypeScript, and Vite; mapping uses d3-geo, TopoJSON, and Natural Earth boundaries. The repository documents 68 unit tests (Vitest) and 33 browser tests (Playwright). GitHub Actions supports deployment to GitHub Pages. Explore the source repository and its NASA data documentation.

Current limits include two ocean dates, one land year (2023), differences between image and numeric-data resolution, and approximately 15–40 seconds to fetch an uncached land location. The tour currently uses browser speech rather than a recorded voice. Future work includes more observation periods, languages, and a NASA FIRMS-based wildfire experience; these are not claimed as implemented.

AI/SI use and attribution

Claude Code (Anthropic; Claude Opus 5.5) assisted with automated testing, debugging, performance work, and documentation under the team's direction and review. Manus AI and ChatGPT helped refine the team's design briefs and prototype notes. Chatterbox AI was used for narration in the submission video, distinct from the browser-based voice in the app.

The team's original concept, the scientific sonification engine core, the NASA measurements, and the deterministic music were not AI-generated. The delivered app's images use NASA SVS/GIBS material and a public-domain Beethoven painting, not AI-generated artwork.

Why it matters

Terraphony gives students, educators, museum visitors, and curious people another way to experience Earth's changing patterns—one that connects hearing, seeing, questioning, and creating. It does not replace scientific data: every meaningful note leads back to a measurable observation.

Composed by Earth. Conducted by you.
